name: Legionarii Armigeri Propugnatores iuniores

abilities.name: Testudo
abilities.text: The troops of this unit raise their shields above their heads in a defensive formation.

abilities.text: The unit moves into close wall formation.

attributes.text: This unit can hide in forests until enemy units get too close.

short: The name Propugnatores means «defenders» or «champions» (zealous defenders). There are still no versions of the origin of this detachment, but the similarity of the shield patterns of a Propugnatores and the Minervii units may provide an important clue. The name Minervii clearly refers to the goddess Minerva, however indirectly through Legio I Minervia. Both could be detachments from the same parent legion, and since Minerva was the goddess of defensive strategy and warfare (as contrasted with the more aggressive and offensive Mars), the title Propugnatores for a unit from Legio I Minervia was quite appropriate. Legio I Minervia seems to have left no trace in the limitanei units of the Notitia Dignitatum, which may indicate that all such units were incorporated into the field army at some point; the several existing Propugnatores detachments according to the Notitia could easily have made up an entire old-style legion. Armigeri (latin) translates as «armored, equipped for war»- it is quite possible that the soldiers of these legions were particularly well protected or armed. According to historians R. Scharf and E.A. Mekhamadiev, the terms seniores and iuniores reflected the process of gradual division of the late Roman legions, which affected several time periods: 353-355, 364 and 395, when from the ranks of the older legions, designated as seniores, were separated new units called iuniores. The formation of iuniores units allowed the sons of soldiers to begin their service in the same privileged military units in which their fathers (seniores) had served, and to advance up the military ranks relatively quickly.
history: In the face of an increasing number of barbarian incursions, the effective defence of Rome’s now-sprawling territory became a serious problem in the 4th century AD. The Emperor Constantine’s controversial solution was to divide the army into two halves. 'Limitanei', literally ‘the men on the limes’ or 'borders', were frontier garrison troops intended to pin down an invading force until the full-time 'comitatenses', the late-Roman equivalent of the traditional Legionaries, could arrive to deal with the situation decisively. Although well-equipped, limitanei were generally considered by all to be second-class warriors. This was possibly because they were often part-time soldiers who had been encouraged to settle and farm the land around their outposts in exchange for policing the Empire's borders.
strengths: Very low damage and armour penetration
